summary: Explains how language tags are attached to values in LDAP directory entries and how servers should interpret them, so the same name or description can be stored in several languages. It was replaced by RFC 3866.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone book entry can say a name in English and also in French. This rule is the label that tells which language each version is written in.

questions: how to mark language in ldap
subtitle: How to label attributes in multiple languages in directory entries.

tldr.problem: Directory entries often store text like names and descriptions in multiple languages, but there was no standard way to label which language each value was written in.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2596 defines a syntax where language codes (like 'en-US' or 'fr') are appended to attribute names using a 'lang-' prefix, so servers and clients know which language each value is in.
tldr.outcome: LDAP implementations can now store and search multilingual directory data consistently. RFC 3866 replaced this standard.

facts.label: Distinguished Names
facts.value: Language codes MUST NOT be used in DNs

today: RFC 2596 was a Proposed Standard. It has been obsoleted by RFC 3866, which consolidated LDAP specifications.

sections.title: The Problem: Storing Names in Multiple Languages
sections.content:
LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is a system for storing and retrieving information about people and resources in a directory. Most directory attributes are human-readable strings like names, addresses, and descriptions. When the same information needs to be stored in multiple languages—such as a person's name in both English and German—there was no standard way to mark which language each version was in.

This RFC describes how language codes can be attached to attribute values to solve that problem. The solution lets servers, clients and applications understand that a given name or description is in a specific language.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a person's name or a company's description is stored in multiple languages. You need a way to say 'this version is in English, that one is in French' so people searching the directory get the right version.

sections.title: Language Codes and the LDAP Syntax
sections.content:
Language codes follow the format defined in RFC 1766, which uses strings of alphabetic characters and hyphens. Examples include en (English), en-US (US English), fr (French), and ja-JP (Japanese).

In LDAP, the language code is part of the AttributeDescription, the full name that includes the base attribute type and its options. The syntax is attributeName;lang-languageCode. For example, givenName;lang-en-US means the given name in US English, while CN;lang-ja means the common name in Japanese. Language codes are case-insensitive, so lang-en-US and lang-EN-US are treated identically.
sections.plainLanguage: A language tag is a simple code like 'en' or 'fr' attached to an attribute name with 'lang-' in front of it. The tag tells you what language that piece of text is written in.

sections.title: Using Language Codes in LDAP Operations
sections.content:
Language codes affect how LDAP servers handle different operations. When a client searches the directory with a language code in the filter, the server only returns attribute values that match both the attribute type and the exact language code. For example, a search for name;lang-en-US=Billy Ray will match name;lang-en-US: Billy Ray and CN;lang-en-us: Billy Ray (since CN is a subtype of name), but not name: Billy Ray (no language tag) or name;lang-en: Billy Ray (different language code).

When adding new entries to the directory, clients can include multiple language-coded versions of the same attribute, and servers that support language codes must accept them. When modifying or comparing attributes, the client must provide the exact language code that matches what is stored in the directory. Language codes are not allowed in Distinguished Names (the directory paths that uniquely identify entries).
sections.plainLanguage: When you search for a name with a language tag, you only get back names with that exact language tag. If you add a new person to the directory, you can give their name in English, French, and German all at once.

sections.title: LDAP vs. X.500 Approach
sections.content: LDAP's language code approach differs from the X.500 directory standard (which uses a more complex mechanism called contexts). LDAP's approach is simpler: clients and servers treat a language-coded attribute as a subtype of the base attribute. The specification references RFC 1766 for language code registration, which allows the IANA to standardize new language codes. Unlike X.500, LDAP forbids language codes in Distinguished Names and does not use a separate administrative procedure for deciding which attribute types can have language codes.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a simpler way to handle language tags than older directory systems used. It lets anyone propose a new language code through a standard process.

sections.title: Limitations and Compliance
sections.content: Servers are only required to accept language codes on attributes; they do not have to store them in the directory. A server that cannot store language codes must treat any attribute with a language code as an unrecognized attribute. The RFC also notes that diagnostic messages from servers should use only printable ASCII characters, since not all clients can display the full Unicode range.
sections.plainLanguage: Some directory servers can store and remember which language each name or description is in. Others just accept the tag but don't remember it, so later the language information is lost.
